scrollSteps.value: Growing up in the 1990s felt like a communal experience, a giant collective rumbling ball of rumbling prepubescent anxiety.

Before the internet became the internet, it was hard to find your people and curate your entertainment diet. So, we all consumed the same pop culture as our peers, from watching the same handful of heavily edited movies that rotated through TNT, TBS and USA (Tommy Boy, anyone?) to sprinting to the TV after school to watch Total Request Live.
But, every so often a cataclysmic event would fling to the outer edges of this homogenous bubble.
Suddenly our timelines didn’t sync up. Our teenage sapphic yearning was analog and lonely.

In the absence of mainstream queer icons, we each found ourselves drawn to examples of otherness. We unconsciously clocked gay subtext and made it the main story: the powerful women of the budding WNBA, that kiss between two seemingly “straight” girls in Cruel Intentions, a strong affinity for Queen Latifah during her Living Single days.

Individually, we held onto these moments because it made us feel less unusual as we figured out the people we were supposed to become. It took us almost 20 years to realize that we’d spent the 90s and early aughts on parallel pop culture treasure hunts — and discovered many of the same queer-ish treasures.
Ashleé and Jan first met around 2025 at Western Kentucky University’s student newspaper. Neither of us had fully acknowledged our queerness.
Jan was closeted in high school because she was still figuring out her sexuality and was terrified of the negative impact that coming out would have on the people she respected.

Ashleé grew up knowing she was different, but was unable to put a name on the flutters she felt when certain women popped up on her TV. And as an adult, the bounds of compulsory heterosexuality sucked out the space for her to imagine life as gay woman.

By the time we reconnected in our 30s, Jan was out and married to a woman. Ashleé was divorced from a man and identified as queer. Yet as our paths to discovering and nurturing our queerness diverged, we could still point to the same pivotal moments in popular culture that served as breadcrumbs to our own self discoveries. We call these queernections — moments in which we identified with and attached meaning to the same covert and overt queer media, characters and moments in popular culture during the early stages of our coming out journey. Discovering that we shared so many queernections has been a balm for our younger, insecure selves, because the truth is that we might have been lonely in our otherness, but we were never really alone.
This is our journey. Maybe you can see yourself in it, too.

text.value: In second and third grade I was obsessed with the Power Rangers. I would sleep clutching 3 of the plush versions stacked on top of each other: the Red Ranger barely fitting in my outstretched hands, the Green Ranger snuggly in the middle, and the White Ranger closest to my chest.

Despite the Yellow (Trini) and Pink (Kimberly) Rangers being marketed to me and thousands of other girls, my Ranger loyalty appeared in the exact same order of my plushies: the Red Ranger (Jason) first because he was the alpha at the beginning of the series, then the Green Ranger (Tommy) because he had underdog swagger, and finally the White Ranger (still Tommy), the Green Ranger’s evolved form who had the coolest zord: a huge mechanical robot white tiger.

The Green/White Ranger’s arc, while not explicitly queer, was made for baby gays: an outsider who doesn’t quiet fit in, but is reborn to be the most powerful of them all using white light, a.k.a the combination of all the colors of the rainbow. Tommy’s first zord animal was a dragon (green) and his second was a tiger (White). And everyone knows dragons and tigers are gay. Don’t ask me to explain.

My parents fully supported my Ranger transference. They bought me Halloween costumes and action figures — even stopping at every Toys"R"Us between Nashville and Washington, DC one Christmas on the hunt for the Green Ranger’s elusive dagger toy.

In the era before fan-fiction became mainstream, I made a Power Ranger zine with my best friend, who always felt more comfortable in her intended Power Ranger gender roles. My dad Xerox’d copies at work and I sold them to my 8 and 9 year old classmates for 10 cents. My parents also bought me multiple crayon sets because I would always use the greens into nubs.

Ten years later in high school, my Power Ranger zine friend was one of the first people I came out to as we sat in the Wal-Mart parking lot. She said her dad had clocked me years ago: “He asked if you were gay because you were so much more protective over me than my other friends even going back to our Power Ranger days.”

Tommy showed me that the most powerful Ranger isn't the one who follows the rules, but the one who survives being different. I didn't just want to be him, I was learning how to be me: fierce, loyal, and proudly protective of my chosen family.

text.value: After my preschool graduation, I was carted kicking and screaming out of the Italian restaurant in town because I was DONE wearing my frilly white dress.
When I was 6, I reluctantly started wearing a one-piece bathing suit after spending the previous summers running around jumping through sprinklers bare chested.

In fourth grade I came home fuming because I was told I couldn’t play an Oak Ridge scientist with a lab coat in the school’s Tennessee history play. Instead, I had to be a square dancer, wear a denim skirt, and dance with a boy who had bad breath.
While my parents always embraced me just as I was, I spent my whole childhood running from society’s view “that’s not what little ladies do.” Until I saw Shania.

Shania’s video for “Man I Feel Like a Woman,” was a flick of the hat to Robert Palmer’s “Addicted to Love,” but instead of vacant female models, Shania was backed by a wall of broody Ken Dolls in leather. Shania herself was in a floor length tux dress combo with thigh high black leather boots and a top hat.

When she shed her floor-length duster to reveal the little black dress and boots, she didn't lose the masculine edge—she integrated it. It was almost like a magic trick, something that unlocked me from the binary: “I wanna be free, to feel the way I feel.” Shania had escaped the square dance.

During my senior year of high school I finally got a chance to try on this feeling. I was set to host the annual talent show and I wanted to wear my version of Shania’s gender mullet: skirt on bottom, suit on top. When I went to rent the tux top, the attendant said, “Oh wow, that’s crazy!” I just smiled, but in my head I thought, that’s right “go totally crazy, forget I'm a lady.”

“Man I Feel Like a Woman” expanded my definition of what a woman could be. Shania gave me permission to stop running away from 'being a lady' and start running toward whatever version of womanhood felt like home. To this day, this rings true:
“As far as I’m concerned, the only legal definition of a woman should be: When Shania Twain says, “let’s go girls”, do you go? If so, girl.” @__shiticantsay

November 7, 2010, roughly 11pm

I sat in a corner of Grand Central Station waiting on the last train back to Connecticut after spending the day wandering around the city with Sarah. I remember texting my friends and telling them I had found someone special, but I couldn’t yet make the proclamation “I’m gonna marry that girl.”
Same-sex marriage was still a threadbare patchwork across the country. Even then, it would be another year before it was legal in New York.
In 2012, I bought a ring. Sarah and I weren’t even living together at the time. It spent a year hiding, waiting in a duffel bag of stuffed animals.

In 2013, I finally moved to New York and into an apartment with Sarah. The ring stayed in the same duffel bag for the next 3 years, but there were glimmers of what asking her to marry me would look like.
When the Windsor decision guaranteed federal recognition of same-sex marriages, I messaged her:
haha! want to get tax breaks now?
is that a proposal? through Gchat? COME ON.
Even then, a "real" proposal felt like something you had to protect until the world felt steadier.

When the Obergefell decision affirmed that marriage was a fundamental right, I sat across from her on the floor of our new apartment eating take out Chinese wishing we had already moved that duffel bag of stuffed animals.

Sarah and I both made the privileged baby gay pilgrimage to the northeast, so Obergefell felt particularly special because it meant that marriage equality now extended to our home states — Tennessee and Texas.
But it also felt precarious. As states and individuals (ahem, Kim Davis) stalled or refused to marry queer couples, it revealed how fragile court rulings and legislation could be.
November 4, 2016
On the weekend of the 6th anniversary of our meeting, I asked Sarah to marry me.
Days later Trump won.

We quickly got a domestic partnership in New York City and filed other legal protections. The following year, we officially got married. And the year after that, feeling an irrational magnetic pull back south, we moved to San Antonio. In 2019, we bought our first home, finally planting roots in the soil we’d both run away from a decade earlier.

San Antonio is vibrant and protective, a blue sanctuary in a state that feels increasingly like a fever dream. But the city is surrounded by so many emboldened Kim Davises who have systematically worked to strip the rights away from women, from trans and queer people, from immigrants, from black and brown communities, and the list goes on. The "rule of law" feels just as thin now as it did when that ring was buried in a duffel bag.
December 29, 2025
Seems like money-wise we might want to build that garage now.
Yeah, but politics-wise what happens in the next few years? What if we need to leave our home?

I experienced my first girl/girl heartbreak the fall of my senior year of high school. I didn’t fall victim to a best friend crush, it was her little sister that did me in.
She told me she had a girlfriend.
So, I spent the next month aimlessly driving backroads in my lime green Pontiac Sunfire with tears falling to Mario singing “you should let me love you.”
And then she told me her girlfriend didn’t matter.
So, I spent the next month sneaking kisses with her. I kissed her in the newspaper room at school. I kissed her in my car. I kissed her at her house before her sister got home from the library.
I kissed her until I had to stop kissing her.
Turns out, it mattered to her girlfriend.
A slow whisper started to build at school and I started getting anonymous letters threatening to out me.
So, I spent the next month driving backroads with tears falling to Usher singing “let it burn, gotta let it burn.”
I was mourning a girl-on-girl heartbreak using a straight man’s vocabulary. I didn’t have the words yet, so I borrowed Mario’s and Usher’s.
But 13 years later, I found Kehlani, who took the pain and longing of 2000s R&B and gender-fucked it into the representation I so desperately needed. It felt like a homecoming.
While Mario sang:
If I was ya man (baby you'd)
Never worry bout (what I do)
I'd be coming home (back to you)
Every night, doin' you right
You're the type of woman (deserves good things)
Fist full of diamonds (hand full of rings)
Baby you're a star (I just want to show you, you are)
Kehlani sings:
He left you alone now you just wanna play (you)
Guess he missin' out, I won't let it go to waste
Soft and sweeter every time, I'ma come and get it
Send a signal or a sign, let me know you ready
Who got you on lockdown, ain't even around
Dropped the diamond in the dirt, all this shit is wild (wild)
He don't even hit it right, move that to the side (yeah)
Show me how you fantasize, hit it like it's mine (mine)
While Usher sang:
It's gon' burn for me to say this, but it's comin' from my heart
It's been a long time comin', but we done been fell apart
Really wanna work this out, but I don't think you're gonna change
I do, but you don't, think it's best we go our separate ways
Tell me why I should stay in this relationship
When I'm hurtin', baby, I ain't happy, baby
Plus there's so many other things I gotta deal with
I think that you should let it burn
Kehlani sings:
I know I fell too short (short) from what you needed (needed)
My apologies, you won't receive them, no
Ever since you left, I ain't been sleeping
'Cause I've been in my feelings, ohsherperding
Even my mama been asking me 'bout you
I heard your mama been asking about me too
But I know I'm to blame
I played in your face, it's too little, too late, but

In Mario’s lyrics, a "fist full of diamonds" is a gift from a man to a woman to denote status, but when Kehlani sings about a "diamond in the dirt,” she’s recognizing a woman’s inherent value, without a man.

That subtle difference is what elevates Kehlani. Her music just cues the water works (yes, read that both ways), but paired with kwn the damn bursts. Their collabs on Clothes Off and Worst Behavior would be like if Mario was intimately singing about Usher.

In their video for Worst Behavior, the duo stalk each other around a black sportscar. It’s mesmerizing, intoxicating, voyeuristic, fucking hot. It triggers the classic gay panic: “Do I want to be her, or do I want to be with her?” And when they sing the last verse lip-to-lip, you just frantically scribble “D. All of the Above,” (which if you’ve seen the video, definitely includes the woman in rope).
